title: Design System: Stanford Health Care Consultation Prototypes

display.purpose: Major decision-stage headings used once per workspace.

title.purpose: Panel headings, cards, and patient identity.

body.purpose: Narrative, evidence, form values, and instructions.

label.purpose: Fields, tabs, statuses, and compact section labels.

shadows.name: floating-workspace
shadows.purpose: Resizable consult board and modal dialog only.

shadows.name: context-separation
shadows.purpose: Separates patient context from scrolling work.

shadows.name: sticky-action-separation
shadows.purpose: Separates sticky bottom actions from form content.

shadows.name: list-card-lift
shadows.purpose: Minimal lift for draggable consult cards.

motion.name: button-press
motion.purpose: Brief physical confirmation on active buttons.

motion.name: recording-pulse
motion.purpose: Used only while the microphone is actively listening.

motion.name: reduced-motion
motion.purpose: Near-zero animation and transition duration under prefers-reduced-motion.

components.name: Local Status Tabs

narrative.overview:
This system should feel like a focused Windows workstation used during real inpatient coordination: compact, explicit, and built to keep patient context and pending work visible. Its visual language is code-led rather than decorative. Cool neutral surfaces, thin structural borders, compact controls, and a single blue action color create familiarity without reproducing any proprietary EHR screen or asset.

The interface is dense but not cramped. Hierarchy comes from persistent context bands, sectional headers, tabular alignment, and restrained semantic color. Clinical decisions remain visible and reviewable: urgency, ownership, uncertainty, pending information, generated content, and final clinician action are presented as text as well as color. Every scenario is synthetic and the persistent synthetic-data label is part of the interface contract.
keyCharacteristics: Windows-native Segoe UI typography with compact, predictable control sizing.
Cool gray-blue structure, white work surfaces, and restrained blue emphasis.
Border-led hierarchy with shadows reserved for floating or modal layers.
Persistent patient context and plain-language status at decision points.
Original components informed by familiar inpatient workflow conventions, never proprietary imitation.

rules.name: The Semantic Rarity Rule
rules.body: Use amber, red, teal, and green only to encode a named state or consequential action; never distribute them as decoration.

rules.name: The Text Plus Color Rule
rules.body: Every state must remain understandable from its label, iconography, or surrounding copy when color is unavailable.

rules.name: The Native Clarity Rule
rules.body: Keep Segoe UI as the first font on Windows and do not introduce display faces, decorative italics, or oversized marketing typography into clinical routes.

rules.name: The Context Before Task Rule
rules.body: Patient identity and encounter context must appear above the editable or actionable workspace and remain visually distinct from it.

rules.name: The Dense, Not Crowded Rule
rules.body: Prefer sectional borders, 8–18px spacing, and aligned columns over oversized whitespace or card grids.

rules.name: The Flat-by-Default Rule
rules.body: If a surface is not floating, sticky, modal, or draggable, separate it with tone and border rather than shadow.

dos: Do keep patient identity, encounter context, synthetic-data labeling, ownership, urgency, pending information, and status visible at the point of action.
Do use compact Segoe UI typography, tabular numerals, aligned grids, and one-pixel dividers to support rapid scanning on Windows and Edge.
Do preserve explicit hover, focus-visible, selected, disabled, error, recording, generating, drag, drop-target, and confirmation states.
Do keep generated content editable and pair it with an explicit clinician-review requirement.
Do use semantic HTML controls, associated labels, keyboard-visible focus, live regions where state changes, and reduced-motion support.
donts: Don't imply that this original prototype is an official Epic product, integration, endorsement, or exact reproduction.
Don't copy proprietary assets or screens, or trade durable clinical context for a consumer-app aesthetic.
Don't use color alone for status, urgency, error, selection, ownership, or completion.
Don't add decorative gradients, glass, large pill controls, oversized marketing type, or shadows to ordinary in-flow panels.
Don't hide uncertainty, pending information, provenance, or the need for clinician review behind generated summaries or automated routing.
